subject: Archaeology
title: The Standard of Ur: War and Peace
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Standard of Ur: War and Peace.

hook.text: A wooden box covered in lapis lazuli and shell mosaics was found crushed in a tomb at Ur — it tells a story on each side.

buildup.text: One side shows war: chariots trampling enemies, soldiers marching prisoners.

discovery.text: The Standard of Ur is from about 2600 BCE. It is one of the earliest known examples of narrative art — a story told in pictures.

twist.text: No one knows what the object actually was. It was too small for a battle standard.

climax.text: The war-and-peace theme appears throughout human art. This 4,600-year-old box captured a duality that has never changed.

punchline.text: War on one side, peace on the other. Sumer understood the human condition 4,600 years ago.

quiz.question: What mystery surrounds the Standard of Ur?
options: The language on it has never been translated
No one knows what the object actually was — it may be a musical instrument's soundbox
It was found in a location hundreds of miles from Ur

details.summary: The Standard of Ur is a mosaic box from around 2600 BCE showing scenes of war and peace on its two sides. One side depicts soldiers, chariots, and prisoners; the other shows feasting, music, and trade — a vivid snapshot of Sumerian life in both its violent and celebratory aspects.
details.whyItMatters: This artifact provides one of the earliest visual narratives of an ancient society. It shows that Sumerian artists could tell complex stories and that warfare and celebration were equally central to their culture.
takeaways: The Standard of Ur dates to around 2600 BCE
Its two sides depict war and peace respectively
It provides one of the earliest visual narratives of society

faq.question: What is the Standard of Ur made of?
faq.answer: Shell, red limestone, and lapis lazuli inlaid into a wooden box with bitumen adhesive. The lapis lazuli came from Afghanistan, showing that Ur had trade connections spanning thousands of kilometers even 4,600 years ago.

faq.question: What was the Standard of Ur used for?
faq.answer: Its purpose is debated. It may have been a ceremonial object, a musical instrument's sound box, or a battle standard carried on a pole. Woolley named it a standard, but its true function remains uncertain.
